content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, a 'sign' (Hebrew 'oth; Greek semeion) is understood as a divinely given event, act, or object that points beyond itself to God's presence, power, and purpose — an attesting pointer that authenticates God's revelation, covenant, or messenger. In the Gospel of John especially, 'signs' are Jesus' miracles understood not as ends in themselves but as revelations of his identity and glory, intended to lead observers to faith. More broadly, a sign functions as a symbol of divine attestation: it confirms a promise (covenant signs), validates a prophet or apostle, or discloses a coming reality (eschatological signs).","primary_basis":["John 2:11 (the first sign at Cana revealing Jesus' glory)","John 20:30-31 (signs written 'that you may believe')","Exodus 4:8-9; 7:3 (signs authenticating Moses before Pharaoh)","Isaiah 7:14 (the sign of Immanuel)","Genesis 9:12-13 (rainbow as sign of the covenant)","Genesis 17:11 (circumcision as sign of the covenant)","Exodus 31:13 (Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel)","Matthew 12:39-40 (the sign of Jonah pointing to the resurrection)","Luke 2:12 (the sign given to the shepherds)","2 Corinthians 12:12 (signs of a true apostle)","Hebrews 2:4 (God bearing witness by signs and wonders)","Genesis 1:14 (heavenly lights 'for signs and seasons')"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Covenant sign and seal: signs (rainbow, circumcision, Sabbath, and by extension baptism and the Lord's Supper) as visible marks and seals of God's covenant promises — the sacramental reading emphasized in Reformed and Catholic theology.","basis":["Genesis 9:12-17","Genesis 17:11","Exodus 31:13,17","Romans 4:11 (circumcision as 'a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith')"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Eschatological portent: signs as heavenly or historical omens announcing the end times, the day of the Lord, or Christ's return ('signs of the times').","basis":["Matthew 16:3","Matthew 24:3,30 (the sign of the Son of Man)","Luke 21:11,25","Joel 2:30-31 / Acts 2:19","Revelation 12:1-3; 15:1"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Authenticating miracle: signs primarily as wonders that validate a divinely commissioned messenger (Moses, the prophets, Jesus, the apostles), with emphasis on the miracle's evidential function.","basis":["Exodus 4:1-9","John 3:2 (Nicodemus: 'no one can do these signs unless God is with him')","Acts 2:22","2 Corinthians 12:12","Mark 16:17-20","Hebrews 2:4"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Negative or judgment-oriented reading: sign-seeking as a mark of unbelief, and signs (including the sign of Jonah) read as warnings of judgment on an unrepentant generation; also deceptive signs performed by false christs and the man of lawlessness.","basis":["Matthew 12:38-39; 16:4 ('an evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign')","1 Corinthians 1:22 ('Jews demand signs')","Matthew 24:24 (false christs performing great signs)","2 Thessalonians 2:9 (lying signs and wonders)","Revelation 13:13-14; 16:14; 19:20 (signs performed by the beast/false prophet)"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Prophetic sign-act: symbolic actions performed by prophets (and their children or bodies) as living signs dramatizing God's message, e.g., Isaiah's children, Ezekiel's enacted parables.","basis":["Isaiah 8:18 ('I and the children the LORD has given me are signs')","Isaiah 20:3","Ezekiel 4:1-3; 12:6,11; 24:24,27"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad, recognizable consensus that 'sign' in Scripture denotes a pointer beyond itself to divine reality — an attesting, revelatory, or covenantal marker rather than a mere marvel. The main interpretive divergences concern emphasis rather than substance: Johannine scholarship stresses signs as christological revelation eliciting faith; sacramental traditions stress covenant signs and seals; apocalyptic and popular prophecy traditions stress eschatological portents; and a corrective strand highlights the biblical critique of sign-seeking and warnings about deceptive signs. Because 'sign' is a broad, multi-context term rather than a single symbol, the consensus is about its function (divine attestation and pointing) rather than a single fixed referent."}
